Usage records belong in a durable, queryable ledger separate from application logs
The write path should stay fast; aggregation/billing queries should run separately from the hot request path
Usage should be recorded even on exception paths so partial failures don't silently drop billing data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Cost tracking enforced at a single chokepoint via decorator/context manager
Tenant ID sourced from enforced request context, not optional args
Records actual provider-returned usage, not pre-call estimates
Handles exception paths so billing data isn't silently lost
Code clarity and correctness

questions.title: Implementing a Guardrail Classifier Gate in the Request Path
questions.prompt: Verdigris Manufacturing wants an input/output guardrail classifier integrated into their internal engineering-knowledge chatbot's request path, not bolted on as an afterthought. Write the integration logic that runs the classifier on both the incoming request and the generated response, and decides whether to block, allow, or flag for review.
questions.modelAnswer:
The integration needs the classifier to run at two distinct points -- before the model call, scoring the incoming request against policy categories, and after generation, scoring the actual output -- because, as with any layered guardrail design, a clean input can still produce a problematic output and vice versa. Each classifier call should return a category and a confidence score rather than a bare boolean, because a single hard threshold collapses useful information: high-confidence violations should block outright, low-confidence borderline cases are better routed to a flagged-for-review queue than either blocked (hurting legitimate users) or silently allowed (defeating the guardrail's purpose).

The implementation below treats the input-check and output-check as two gates in the same pipeline, short-circuiting before the (expensive) model call if the input gate blocks, and only committing to 'allowed' after both gates pass. It separates the policy decision (block/allow/flag) from the raw classifier score so the threshold logic is centralized and auditable in one place rather than scattered, and it logs every classifier decision -- including allows -- so the false-positive/false-negative rate can be measured and the thresholds tuned from real data rather than guessed once and left alone.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd build this so the classifier gate is structurally part of the request pipeline, not a side-call someone has to remember to invoke. Input gets scored first, and if that comes back as a high-confidence violation, we short-circuit before ever paying for the model call -- there's no reason to generate a response to something we're going to block anyway. If the input passes, we generate, then score the actual output, because a perfectly fine-looking question can still produce a problematic answer and that's a distinct failure mode input screening can't catch.

The design choice I'd defend in review is returning a score and category from the classifier instead of a flat yes/no, because that lets me have three outcomes instead of two -- block the clear violations, allow the clear clean cases, and route the genuinely ambiguous middle into a human-review queue instead of forcing a binary call I don't have confidence in. And I'd log every decision, including the allows, because that's the only way we ever get real data to tell us if our thresholds are too loose or too strict -- without that, we're tuning this blind.
commonMistakes: Running the classifier only on input or only on output instead of both
Using a bare boolean block/allow instead of a score, collapsing the ability to route ambiguous cases to review
Generating the model response before checking the input gate, wasting cost on requests that get blocked anyway
Not logging allowed (non-blocked) decisions, losing the data needed to tune thresholds from real traffic
Hardcoding thresholds once with no mechanism to revisit them against measured false-positive/negative rates
keyPoints: Guardrail classification should run on both input and output as two distinct gates
Classifier output should be a score/category, not a bare boolean, enabling a block/allow/flag-for-review decision
The input gate should short-circuit before the model call to avoid wasted generation cost on blocked requests
Threshold/policy logic should be centralized and auditable rather than scattered across call sites
All classifier decisions, including allows, should be logged to enable ongoing threshold tuning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Implements both input and output gates distinctly
Uses score/category output enabling a flag-for-review path, not just binary block/allow
Short-circuits before model call on input violation
Logs decisions for threshold tuning; code is clear and correct

questions.title: Writing a Circuit Breaker for a Flaky Model Provider API
questions.prompt: Sablewood Finance's portfolio-insights assistant calls a third-party model API that occasionally degrades -- elevated error rates or timeouts lasting minutes at a time. Without protection, every request during a degradation retries and times out slowly, backing up the whole service. Write a circuit breaker wrapper around the model API call that fails fast during a degradation and recovers automatically.
questions.modelAnswer:
A circuit breaker tracks the recent failure rate of calls to a dependency and flips between three states: closed (calls go through normally), open (calls fail immediately without even attempting the real call, because the dependency is known to be degraded), and half-open (a small number of trial calls are let through to test if the dependency has recovered, before fully closing again). The point of failing fast in the open state is that retrying a slow-failing dependency doesn't just fail that one request slowly, it holds a thread/connection and consumes capacity in your own service for the duration of each doomed attempt, which is exactly how one degraded dependency turns into a full outage of your own system.

The implementation below trips to open after a failure-rate threshold is crossed within a rolling window (not after a single failure, since a handful of failures during a window with a lot of traffic might just be normal background noise), stays open for a cooldown period, then moves to half-open and lets a limited number of probe requests through -- if those succeed, it closes; if they fail, it reopens and resets the cooldown. Critically, when the circuit is open, the caller needs a defined fallback (a cached last-known response, a clear 'temporarily unavailable' response, or routing to a backup model) rather than just an exception bubbling up to the end user, because failing fast only helps the rest of the system if there's somewhere sensible for that fast failure to go.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd frame the whole point of this up front: without a circuit breaker, a degraded third-party API doesn't just make requests slow, it actively endangers our own service, because every request that retries against a slow-failing dependency ties up our own capacity waiting on it. The breaker's job is to notice the dependency is unhealthy and stop sending it traffic for a while, failing fast instead of failing slow.

I'd implement the standard three-state pattern -- closed, open, half-open -- and I'd specifically trip based on a failure rate over a rolling window, not a single failure, because with real traffic volume a few failures in a short window can be completely normal. Once it's open, I wouldn't just let exceptions bubble up to the user; I'd design a fallback path -- maybe a cached last answer, maybe a clear 'try again shortly' message -- because the entire value of failing fast evaporates if the fast failure still produces a bad experience with nowhere better to go. And half-open is the part I'd walk through carefully in review: it's not 'fully open again,' it's a small number of probe requests testing recovery, so one lucky success doesn't flip us back to full traffic before we're actually sure the dependency recovered.
commonMistakes: Tripping the circuit on a single failure instead of a failure rate over a rolling window
Letting exceptions bubble up to the user with no defined fallback when the circuit is open
Implementing only closed/open with no half-open probing step, so recovery requires a full cooldown with no verification
Fully reopening to 100% traffic on the first successful probe instead of gradually confirming recovery
Not distinguishing circuit-breaker failures from normal application errors in monitoring/alerting
keyPoints: A circuit breaker has three states: closed (normal), open (fail fast), half-open (probe for recovery)
Tripping should be based on failure rate over a rolling window, not a single failure
Failing fast in the open state protects the caller's own service capacity, not just the user experience
A defined fallback (cache, backup model, clear message) is required when the circuit is open
Half-open should use limited probe traffic before fully closing, to avoid premature full recovery

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Implements the closed/open/half-open state machine correctly
Trips on rolling failure rate, not single failures
Includes a defined fallback path for the open state
Half-open uses limited probing before fully closing
Code clarity and correctness

questions.title: Building an Automated Eval Harness Skeleton for CI
questions.prompt: Tallgrass Logistics wants every prompt or model change to its route-optimization explainer run against a golden eval set automatically in CI, blocking the merge if quality regresses beyond a tolerance, instead of relying on a human to remember to spot-check. Write the skeleton for an automated eval harness that runs on every pull request.
questions.modelAnswer:
An automated eval harness for CI needs three structural pieces: a fixed golden set loaded from version control (so the test data is reviewed and diffed like code, not a mutable live file that could silently change), a run step that executes the candidate prompt/model against every item and scores it against a rubric or reference, and a comparison step against a stored baseline score so the gate is 'did this regress relative to the last known-good baseline,' not an absolute pass/fail against a fixed number that might not fit every golden-set item equally. The CI gate should fail the build if the aggregate score drops below the baseline by more than an agreed tolerance, and should also surface per-item regressions, not just the aggregate, because an aggregate score can hold steady while quietly failing on a specific category of cases (a change that improves the common case but breaks a known hard case).

The skeleton below keeps the scoring function pluggable (exact-match, embedding similarity, or an LLM-judge call) since different projects and even different items within one golden set may need different scoring approaches, and it writes results to a report artifact so a failed CI run gives a reviewer the specific failing items and their outputs, not just a red X -- a CI gate that just says 'eval failed' with no detail gets bypassed or ignored the first time it's inconvenient, while one that shows exactly what broke gets taken seriously.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd design this so the golden set itself lives in version control right alongside the prompts, because I want any change to the test data to go through the same review and diff process as a code change -- a golden set that can be silently edited defeats the entire purpose of having a fixed baseline to compare against. The harness runs the candidate against every item, scores it, and compares the aggregate against a stored baseline score with an agreed tolerance, rather than some arbitrary fixed pass/fail number that doesn't account for natural variance in the set.

The thing I'd insist on in review is per-item regression reporting, not just an aggregate pass/fail, because I've seen aggregate scores hold steady while a specific category of hard cases quietly breaks -- if the harness only reports the aggregate, that regression ships and nobody notices until it shows up in production. So the CI output needs to name the specific failing items and show the actual output next to the expected one, because a red X with no detail is the kind of check that gets disabled the first time someone's in a hurry.
commonMistakes: Storing the golden set as a mutable file that isn't versioned/reviewed alongside code changes
Gating on an absolute fixed score instead of a regression check against a stored baseline with tolerance
Reporting only an aggregate score, hiding category-specific regressions that the aggregate can mask
Making the scoring function rigid/hardcoded instead of pluggable for different scoring approaches
Producing a pass/fail signal with no detail, making the check easy to ignore or bypass under deadline pressure
keyPoints: The golden set should be version-controlled and reviewed like code, not a mutable live file
The CI gate should compare against a stored baseline with tolerance, not an arbitrary fixed threshold
Per-item regression reporting is needed since aggregate scores can mask category-specific breakage
The scoring function should be pluggable to support different scoring approaches per item or project
A failed run should produce a detailed report (specific failing items, actual vs. expected), not just a pass/fail flag

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Golden set is versioned, not a mutable live artifact
Gate compares against stored baseline with tolerance, not an arbitrary absolute score
Reports per-item regressions, not only an aggregate
Scoring function is pluggable; code is clear and correct

questions.title: Writing a Per-Tenant Rate Limiter with Quota Enforcement
questions.prompt: Perrin Robotics' shared diagnostics-assistant platform has had incidents where one client's traffic spike exhausted model-API rate limits for every other client. Write a per-tenant rate limiter that enforces individual quotas so one tenant's usage spike cannot starve the others.
questions.modelAnswer:
A rate limiter that only enforces a global limit protects the service as a whole but does nothing to prevent one tenant from consuming the entire shared budget, which is exactly the failure mode described. The fix is a per-tenant quota layered underneath the global limit: each tenant gets their own token bucket (or sliding-window counter) sized to their allocated share, so a burst from one tenant is capped at their own bucket regardless of how much global headroom exists, and the global limit remains as a second, outer check protecting the shared downstream dependency from aggregate overload even when every tenant is individually within quota.

The implementation below uses a token-bucket per tenant (refilling at a steady rate, capped at a burst size) because it naturally allows short bursts within a tenant's allocation while still enforcing a steady-state rate, which fits typical request patterns better than a hard fixed-window counter that can allow a full quota's worth of traffic in the last second of one window and the first second of the next. It also separates 'tenant over quota' (a 429 response specific to that tenant, with a retry-after hint) from 'global capacity exhausted' (a different, system-wide signal) so that when alerts fire, it's clear whether a specific tenant is misbehaving or the whole system is under real capacity pressure -- which matters a lot for incident response, since those two conditions need completely different responses.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd point out first that a global-only rate limiter is exactly how we got the incident in the first place -- it protects the service in aggregate but has zero concept of fairness between tenants, so one tenant's spike can eat the whole budget while everyone else gets starved and we can't even tell from the global metric which tenant caused it. The fix is giving every tenant their own quota enforced independently, with the global limit staying in place underneath as a second layer protecting the actual downstream dependency.

I'd implement each tenant's quota as a token bucket rather than a fixed window counter, specifically because fixed windows have that edge-of-window burst problem where a tenant can effectively get two windows' worth of traffic through back-to-back around the boundary. And I'd make sure the two failure signals are distinguishable in monitoring -- a 429 because *this specific tenant* is over their quota is a completely different incident than the system running low on global capacity, and conflating those into one alert makes on-call diagnosis slower than it needs to be.
commonMistakes: Enforcing only a global rate limit with no per-tenant quota, allowing one tenant to starve others
Using a fixed-window counter that allows a burst-at-the-boundary exploit instead of a token bucket or sliding window
Not distinguishing a per-tenant quota breach from global capacity exhaustion in monitoring/alerting
Sizing every tenant's quota identically regardless of their actual allocated share or contract tier
Having no retry-after or backoff signal for a throttled tenant, leading to naive immediate retries that worsen the spike
keyPoints: Per-tenant quotas must be enforced independently from (and underneath) any global rate limit
A token bucket handles bursty traffic more fairly than a fixed-window counter, avoiding boundary-burst exploits
Per-tenant quota breaches and global capacity exhaustion are distinct conditions that should alert differently
Quota size should reflect each tenant's actual allocation, not a uniform default
A throttled response should include a retry-after signal to avoid naive immediate-retry storms

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Implements independent per-tenant quota enforcement, not just a global limit
Uses a token bucket or equivalent avoiding fixed-window boundary bursts
Distinguishes per-tenant throttling from global capacity exhaustion
Code clarity, correctness, and retry-after handling

questions.title: Writing a Retrieval-Freshness Refresh Job for a RAG Index
questions.prompt: Coldharbor Security's threat-advisory RAG assistant retrieves from an index of vendor security bulletins that update throughout the day. Write the incremental refresh job that detects changed or new source documents and updates only those in the vector index, without re-embedding the entire corpus on every run.
questions.modelAnswer:
An incremental refresh job needs a cheap way to detect which source documents actually changed since the last run, which means tracking a content hash or last-modified timestamp per source document and comparing against what was recorded at last index time, rather than re-fetching and re-embedding everything to find out what's different -- re-embedding the full corpus on every run doesn't scale and burns compute on the vast majority of documents that didn't change. For each source that's new or changed, the job re-chunks just that document, re-embeds just those chunks, and upserts them into the vector index keyed by a stable chunk ID, while explicitly deleting any chunks belonging to a source document that was removed or superseded -- that deletion step is often the one people forget, leaving stale chunks from a retracted bulletin permanently retrievable even after the source is gone.

The implementation below separates change-detection (cheap, runs frequently) from the actual re-embed-and-upsert work (more expensive, only runs on what changed), tracks per-document metadata (hash, last-indexed time, source ID) in a small tracking table separate from the vector index itself so the job can answer 'what changed' without querying the vector store, and makes the upsert idempotent by chunk ID so re-running the job after a partial failure doesn't create duplicate chunks.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd design this so the expensive part -- actually re-embedding -- only ever touches documents that changed, and the way I'd detect that cheaply is a content hash stored per source document from the last time it was indexed. Every run, I pull the current hash for each source, compare it against what's on record, and only the documents where that hash differs get re-chunked and re-embedded. That's the difference between a job that scales and one that doesn't once the bulletin volume grows.

The detail I'd call out specifically, because it's the one teams tend to miss, is handling deletions and supersessions -- if a vendor retracts or replaces a bulletin, the old chunks need to be explicitly removed from the index, not just left there because nothing re-embedded over them. I'd also make the upsert idempotent by a stable chunk ID, specifically so that if this job fails halfway through and reruns, we don't end up with duplicate chunks for the same content sitting in the index.
commonMistakes: Re-embedding the entire corpus on every run instead of detecting and processing only changed documents
Using document fetch time instead of a content hash/last-modified check, missing content changes with no timestamp change
Not handling deleted or superseded source documents, leaving stale chunks permanently retrievable
Making the upsert non-idempotent, risking duplicate chunks if the job reruns after a partial failure
Storing change-detection metadata inside the vector index itself instead of a separate lightweight tracking table
keyPoints: Change detection should use a content hash or reliable last-modified signal, checked cheaply before any re-embedding
Only changed or new documents should be re-chunked and re-embedded, not the full corpus
Deleted or superseded source documents must have their chunks explicitly removed from the index
Upserts should be idempotent by a stable chunk ID to tolerate reruns after partial failures
Tracking metadata should live separately from the vector index to keep change detection cheap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Implements cheap, hash-based change detection before any re-embedding
Only processes changed/new documents, not the full corpus
Handles deletions/supersessions explicitly
Idempotent upsert by stable chunk ID; code clarity

questions.title: Debugging a Broken Prompt-Versioning Rollback Script
questions.prompt: Ashgrove Retail's prompt-management system lets engineers roll back a production prompt template to a previous version, but the last rollback didn't actually change the live behavior even though the script reported success. Here is the rollback function. Find the bug and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
The bug is a caching problem disguised as a logic problem: the rollback function correctly updates the stored prompt-version pointer in the database, and that part genuinely succeeds, which is why it reports success truthfully -- but the live request path reads the active prompt template from an in-memory cache that's populated once at service startup and only invalidated on a separate, explicit cache-refresh call that this rollback script never makes. So the database says version 3 is active, but every running instance keeps serving whatever template was cached at boot, which in this case was version 4, and nothing in the rollback path touches that cache at all.

This is a common and dangerous class of bug specifically because the rollback script's own success signal (did the database write succeed) is disconnected from the actual thing the operator cares about (did production behavior change), so the tooling lies by omission -- it's technically correct and practically useless. The fix has two parts: the rollback function itself must call the cache invalidation/broadcast step as part of the same operation, not as a separate manual step an operator has to remember, and the success response should be strengthened to confirm the new version is actually being served (for example, by checking a health/version-reporting endpoint across live instances) rather than just confirming the database write committed -- because 'wrote to the database' and 'changed production behavior' are not the same guarantee, and conflating them is exactly how this incident happened.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd walk through this by not trusting the function's own success report and instead asking what actually serves a live request versus what this script actually touched. The script updates the database pointer, and that write genuinely succeeds -- which is why it reports success -- but the thing serving production traffic is an in-memory cache on each running instance, populated at startup, and nothing in this rollback path tells that cache to refresh. So the database says one thing, every live instance is still doing another, and the rollback 'succeeded' in a sense that has nothing to do with what the operator actually needed.

The fix I'd make is twofold: first, bake the cache invalidation into the rollback operation itself so it's not a second manual step that's easy to forget under incident pressure; second, I'd change what 'success' actually means here -- instead of just confirming the database write committed, I'd have it verify against a live version-reporting endpoint that instances are actually serving the new version before reporting success. That second part matters because this bug is exactly the kind where the tooling's own confidence is misleading -- it told the engineer it worked, truthfully, about the wrong thing.
commonMistakes: Trusting that a database write succeeding means production behavior changed, without checking the live serving path
Not identifying the in-memory cache as a separate state from the database that the rollback never touches
Fixing it by just manually busting the cache once instead of folding invalidation into the rollback operation itself
Leaving the success signal tied only to the database write instead of verifying actual live behavior changed
Assuming a single successful rollback test means the fix is complete without checking all live instances report the new version
keyPoints: The bug is a cache-invalidation gap: the DB pointer updates but live instances serve a separate, stale in-memory cache
A rollback/deployment operation's reported success must reflect actual live behavior, not just a database write
Cache invalidation should be part of the same atomic operation, not a separate manual step
Verifying success should check a live version-reporting signal across instances, not just the write path
This class of bug (tooling truthfully reports the wrong signal) is dangerous because it hides the real failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the cache-invalidation gap as the root cause
Explains why the reported 'success' was misleading
Proposes folding invalidation into the rollback operation itself
Proposes verifying actual live behavior, not just the DB write

questions.title: Writing a Token-Budget Enforcer for Context Assembly
questions.prompt: Oxbow Analytics' document-QA assistant occasionally blows past the model's context window when a user's conversation history plus retrieved chunks plus the system prompt add up to more tokens than the model can accept, causing a hard API error mid-conversation. Write a token-budget enforcer that assembles the final prompt within a fixed budget, trimming intelligently rather than failing.
questions.code:
def assemble_prompt(system_prompt: str, history: list[str], retrieved_chunks: list[dict],
                     current_turn: str, model_context_limit: int, output_reserve: int = 1000,
                     tokenizer=real_model_tokenizer) -> tuple[str, dict]:
    budget = model_context_limit - output_reserve  # leave room for the response itself
    trim_log = []

    system_tokens = tokenizer.count(system_prompt)
    current_tokens = tokenizer.count(current_turn)
    fixed_cost = system_tokens + current_tokens  # non-negotiable content

    chunks = sorted(retrieved_chunks, key=lambda c: c["relevance_score"], reverse=True)
    history_ordered = list(history)  # oldest first, assumed chronological

    def total_tokens():
        chunk_tok = sum(tokenizer.count(c["text"]) for c in chunks)
        hist_tok = sum(tokenizer.count(h) for h in history_ordered)
        return fixed_cost + chunk_tok + hist_tok

    # Priority 1: drop oldest history first
    while total_tokens() > budget and history_ordered:
        dropped = history_ordered.pop(0)
        trim_log.append({"dropped": "history_turn", "preview": dropped[:60]})

    # Priority 2: drop lowest-relevance retrieved chunks
    while total_tokens() > budget and chunks:
        dropped = chunks.pop()  # lowest relevance is last after the sort above
        trim_log.append({"dropped": "retrieved_chunk", "source": dropped.get("source_id")})

    if total_tokens() > budget:
        raise ValueError("Budget exceeded even after trimming all droppable content; "
                          "system prompt + current turn alone exceed the model's context limit")

    assembled = build_final_prompt(system_prompt, history_ordered, chunks, current_turn)
    if trim_log:
        logger.info("Prompt trimmed to fit budget", extra={"trim_log": trim_log})

    return assembled, {"trim_log": trim_log, "final_tokens": total_tokens()}
questions.modelAnswer:
A token-budget enforcer needs a clear priority order for what gets trimmed first when the assembled prompt would exceed budget, because not all content is equally disposable: the system prompt and the current user turn are generally non-negotiable (trimming those breaks the interaction entirely), retrieved RAG chunks are valuable but individually droppable (losing the lowest-relevance chunk degrades quality gracefully rather than catastrophically), and older conversation history is the most disposable since a summarized or dropped early turn is usually tolerable if the recent turns and retrieved context are intact. The enforcer should compute the actual token count of each component using the real tokenizer for the target model -- not a word-count approximation, which can be off by a large margin and is exactly the kind of estimate that causes budget calculations to be wrong in production -- and apply trimming in that priority order until the total fits within a safety margin under the model's actual limit, not right up against the hard limit, since the model's response itself also needs output token headroom.

The implementation below computes per-component token counts up front, defines an explicit trim order (oldest history first, then lowest-scored retrieved chunks, never the system prompt or current turn), and stops trimming as soon as the budget is satisfied rather than over-trimming -- it also logs when trimming occurred and what was dropped, because silent trimming that degrades an answer's grounding without any record makes a later quality complaint ('why did it ignore that document') impossible to debug.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by establishing a priority order for what's allowed to get cut, because the alternative -- failing the whole request with a hard error -- is strictly worse for the user than quietly dropping the least important content and still answering. System prompt and the user's current message are off-limits; those are what makes the interaction work at all. Retrieved chunks are valuable but individually droppable, so if I have to cut something there, I drop the lowest-relevance chunk first. Older conversation history is the most disposable of all -- a summarized or dropped early turn rarely breaks the current exchange.

The implementation detail I'd insist on is using the actual tokenizer for whatever model we're calling, not a word-count estimate, because I've seen those estimates be wrong by enough to make the whole budget calculation meaningless. And I'd build in a safety margin below the model's real limit, not right up against it, since the response itself needs token room too. The other thing I'd push for is logging every time trimming actually happens and exactly what got dropped -- because if we ever get a complaint that the assistant 'ignored' a document, I want to be able to check whether it was silently trimmed for budget reasons rather than guessing.
commonMistakes: Using a word-count approximation instead of the actual model tokenizer, producing inaccurate budget calculations
Trimming the system prompt or current user turn instead of only disposable content (history, low-relevance chunks)
Budgeting right up against the model's hard context limit with no margin for the response's own output tokens
Trimming silently with no logging of what was dropped, making later quality issues impossible to debug
Failing the request with a hard error instead of trimming gracefully when the assembled prompt exceeds budget
keyPoints: Content should be trimmed in a defined priority order: history first, then low-relevance chunks, never system prompt or current turn
Token counts must use the real model tokenizer, not a word-count approximation
A safety margin below the hard context limit is needed to leave room for the model's output tokens
Trimming decisions should be logged so dropped content can be traced during later debugging
Graceful trimming should replace hard failure whenever the assembled prompt would exceed budget

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Defines a sound, prioritized trim order protecting system prompt/current turn
Uses the real tokenizer, not an approximation
Leaves a safety margin for output tokens
Logs trimming decisions for debuggability; code clarity

questions.title: Writing a Cost-Attribution Query Across Tenants and Models
questions.prompt: Garnet Health's finance team asks for a report: total LLM spend per department for last month, broken down by model tier, with departments flagged if their spend grew more than 40% month-over-month. Write the SQL against the usage_records table (tenant_id, department, model, input_tokens, output_tokens, cost_usd, created_at) to produce this.
questions.code:
WITH current_month AS (
  SELECT
    department,
    model,
    SUM(cost_usd) AS total_cost
  FROM usage_records
  WHERE created_at >= date_trunc('month', CURRENT_DATE)
    AND created_at <  date_trunc('month', CURRENT_DATE) + INTERVAL '1 month'
  GROUP BY department, model
),
prior_month AS (
  SELECT
    department,
    model,
    SUM(cost_usd) AS total_cost
  FROM usage_records
  WHERE created_at >= date_trunc('month', CURRENT_DATE) - INTERVAL '1 month'
    AND created_at <  date_trunc('month', CURRENT_DATE)
  GROUP BY department, model
),
dept_totals_current AS (
  SELECT department, SUM(total_cost) AS dept_cost FROM current_month GROUP BY department
),
dept_totals_prior AS (
  SELECT department, SUM(total_cost) AS dept_cost FROM prior_month GROUP BY department
)
SELECT
  c.department,
  c.model,
  c.total_cost AS current_month_cost,
  p.total_cost AS prior_month_cost,
  dc.dept_cost AS department_current_total,
  dp.dept_cost AS department_prior_total,
  CASE
    WHEN dp.dept_cost IS NULL OR dp.dept_cost = 0 THEN NULL  -- avoid divide-by-zero; flagged separately below
    ELSE ROUND(((dc.dept_cost - dp.dept_cost) / dp.dept_cost) * 100, 1)
  END AS department_mom_growth_pct,
  CASE
    WHEN dp.dept_cost IS NULL OR dp.dept_cost = 0 THEN 'new_spend_no_prior_baseline'
    WHEN ((dc.dept_cost - dp.dept_cost) / dp.dept_cost) > 0.40 THEN 'flagged_high_growth'
    ELSE 'normal'
  END AS growth_flag
FROM current_month c
LEFT JOIN prior_month p
  ON c.department = p.department AND c.model = p.model
LEFT JOIN dept_totals_current dc ON c.department = dc.department
LEFT JOIN dept_totals_prior dp ON c.department = dp.department
ORDER BY c.department, c.model;
questions.modelAnswer:
This query needs two time windows compared against each other (last month and the month before), aggregated per department and model tier, with the month-over-month growth computed as a derived value and a flag applied based on that growth -- which means building the current-month and prior-month aggregates separately, joining them on department, and computing the percentage change rather than trying to do it all in a single ungrouped pass. Using a CTE for each month's aggregate keeps the logic readable and makes it easy to verify each piece independently, versus a single deeply nested query that's hard to validate.

A few correctness details matter here: the growth percentage calculation needs to guard against division by zero for a department with no spend in the prior month (which would otherwise either error or produce a misleading infinite percentage), and 'last month' and 'the month before' need to be computed relative to the actual current date rather than hardcoded month boundaries, so the report keeps working correctly as time moves forward. The model-tier breakdown is a straightforward additional grouping dimension alongside department, not a separate query, since finance wants spend sliced by both dimensions in one report.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd build this as two clearly separated monthly aggregates joined together, rather than one complex query trying to do everything at once, because that's much easier for finance (or me, six months from now) to actually verify is correct. First CTE: this month's spend by department and model tier. Second CTE: last month's, same grouping. Then join them on department and model, and compute the percentage change.

The detail I'd double check before handing this over is the division-by-zero case -- if a department had zero spend last month and any spend this month, a naive percentage-growth calculation either errors or reports something like infinity percent, which isn't useful and isn't what finance is asking for; I'd handle that explicitly, probably by flagging it as 'new spend' rather than a growth percentage. And I'd make sure the date ranges are computed relative to today rather than hardcoded, so this report doesn't need to be edited by hand every month it's run.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding specific month date literals instead of computing ranges relative to the current date
Not guarding against division by zero when a department had no prior-month spend
Computing the 40% growth flag without grouping by model tier, losing the requested breakdown
Using a single deeply nested query instead of clear, independently verifiable CTEs for each month
Comparing totals across departments instead of within the same department across the two time periods
keyPoints: Current-month and prior-month aggregates should be computed separately, then joined for comparison
Growth percentage must guard against division by zero for departments with no prior-month spend
Date ranges should be computed relative to the current date, not hardcoded
Model-tier should be a grouping dimension alongside department, not a separate report
CTEs improve readability and let each aggregate be verified independently
