questions.title: Running Your First Architecture Review as the Senior Engineer in the Room
questions.prompt: Tell me about the first time you ran (not just attended) an architecture review as the senior or most experienced engineer in the room. What did you do differently than when you were a reviewer or participant, and what did you learn about the difference between those two roles?
questions.modelAnswer:
The most revealing part of this question is whether the candidate actually recognizes a real difference between being a strong technical contributor in a review and running one, because those are genuinely different skills -- running a review well means managing the room's dynamics (making sure a junior engineer's good point doesn't get steamrolled by a louder senior voice, keeping the discussion from drifting into an unrelated tangent, knowing when to let a disagreement play out versus when to table it and follow up offline) as much as it means having the right technical opinions, and a candidate who only describes the technical content of the review without any awareness of facilitation is missing half of what the question is actually probing.

A strong answer describes a specific concrete change in behavior between participating and running: deliberately asking a quieter engineer a direct question to draw out their perspective rather than assuming silence means agreement, explicitly summarizing where the group landed before moving to the next topic so the review doesn't just end in ambiguous diffusion, or recognizing a moment where the conversation was about to become unproductive (two people repeating the same point with increasing frustration) and redirecting it. Equally important is honesty about something that didn't go well the first time -- a Staff-level candidate who claims their first review as facilitator went flawlessly is either not being candid or wasn't paying close enough attention to notice their own mistakes, and the specific lesson they took from a misstep (letting a conversation run too long without redirecting, failing to make sure a decision was actually recorded afterward) is often more informative than a smooth success story.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd be honest that running a review is a genuinely different skill from being a strong voice in one, and I'd want to describe a specific moment where that difference actually showed up for me, not just assert it in the abstract. As a participant, my job was mostly to have good technical opinions and argue for them well. As the person running it, I noticed I had to actively manage the room -- making sure a quieter or more junior person's point actually got heard and not just talked over by whoever was loudest, and explicitly summarizing where we'd landed before we moved on, because I learned the hard way that a review can feel productive in the room and then nobody's actually sure afterward what was decided.

I'd also want to be upfront about something that didn't go smoothly the first time I ran one, because I think pretending it went perfectly isn't believable and isn't actually useful to talk about. I'd describe a specific misstep -- maybe letting two people go back and forth on the same point for too long before redirecting, or not following up afterward to make sure the decision actually got written down somewhere -- and what I changed the next time because of it.
commonMistakes: Describing only the technical content of the review with no awareness of facilitation as a distinct skill
Claiming the first time running a review went flawlessly, with no honest account of a misstep
Not describing a specific, concrete behavioral difference between participating and facilitating
Missing the importance of explicitly summarizing/recording decisions so the review doesn't end in ambiguity
Describing facilitation only in terms of controlling the conversation rather than drawing out quieter voices
keyPoints: Running a review well requires managing group dynamics, not just having strong technical opinions
Drawing out quieter or more junior voices deliberately is a distinct facilitation skill from arguing a technical point
Explicitly summarizing conclusions before moving on prevents a review from ending in ambiguous diffusion
Recognizing and redirecting an unproductive repetitive disagreement is a facilitation responsibility
Honest acknowledgment of a real misstep the first time is a stronger signal than a claimed flawless outcome

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clearly distinguishes facilitation skills from technical-contributor skills
Describes a specific, concrete behavioral change when running vs. participating
Gives an honest account of a real misstep and what was learned
Shows awareness of group dynamics (quieter voices, drift, decision clarity)

questions.title: Mentoring a Struggling Engineer Through a Hard Technical Problem
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you mentored an engineer who was genuinely stuck on a hard technical problem -- not a quick question, but something they'd been struggling with for a while. How did you approach helping them, and how did you decide how much to just tell them versus how much to let them work through themselves?
questions.modelAnswer:
The core tension this question probes is the balance between efficiency (just telling someone the answer, which solves the immediate problem fastest) and actual skill development (guiding them to find it themselves, which takes longer but builds the capability to solve the next hard problem without help) -- and a strong answer shows the candidate actually thought about that tradeoff deliberately rather than defaulting to one extreme out of habit. A candidate who says 'I just explained the solution' every time is optimizing purely for short-term throughput and isn't actually mentoring; a candidate who insists on pure Socratic questioning even when the engineer is stuck on something genuinely unfamiliar to them (not something they have the background to derive, just haven't yet) is prioritizing the appearance of mentoring over actually being useful and can come across as withholding help for its own sake.

The strongest answers describe reading the specific situation -- was this engineer missing a piece of fundamental background knowledge (in which case direct teaching of that specific gap, not just redirecting them to go struggle more, is the right move), or did they have everything they needed and just hadn't connected the pieces yet (in which case a well-placed question or hint that lets them get the insight themselves is more valuable long-term) -- and adjusting approach accordingly rather than using the same technique regardless of what was actually causing the stuck-ness. Equally telling is whether the candidate checked in on how the engineer was doing emotionally during a long stretch of being stuck, since being stuck on a hard problem for a while is genuinely demoralizing, and a mentor who only addressed the technical gap while ignoring that the person was also frustrated or losing confidence is missing half of what good mentoring actually requires.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd describe a specific case and be honest about how I actually decided the telling-versus-guiding balance in the moment, because I don't think there's one right answer to that tradeoff -- it depends on what's actually causing someone to be stuck. If they're missing a piece of fundamental knowledge they genuinely don't have yet, I don't think making them struggle to rediscover that from scratch is good mentoring, that's just withholding help -- I'd teach that specific gap directly. But if they actually had everything they needed and just hadn't connected the dots, I'd lean toward a well-placed question or hint rather than handing them the answer, because that's the situation where guiding them to the insight themselves actually builds something that'll help them on the next hard problem too.

I'd want to describe how I figured out which situation I was actually in, because that diagnosis is the real skill here, not picking a style and applying it uniformly. And I'd specifically mention checking in on how they were doing, not just technically -- being stuck on something hard for a while is genuinely discouraging, and I think part of mentoring well is noticing when someone's confidence is taking a hit from being stuck, not just focused on closing the technical gap and assuming the person's morale will take care of itself.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to always just explaining the answer directly regardless of what's actually causing the engineer to be stuck
Insisting on pure Socratic questioning even when the engineer is missing fundamental background knowledge they don't yet have
Using the same mentoring technique uniformly instead of diagnosing what's actually causing the specific stuck-ness
Focusing only on closing the technical gap while ignoring the engineer's morale/confidence during a long stuck period
Describing the mentoring approach only in the abstract without a specific situation or concrete outcome
keyPoints: The telling-vs-guiding balance should be decided based on what's actually causing the stuck-ness, not applied uniformly
A missing fundamental knowledge gap often warrants direct teaching, not forced rediscovery
A connect-the-dots gap (engineer has what they need but hasn't synthesized it) often warrants guided questioning instead
Good mentoring includes attending to the engineer's morale/confidence, not just the technical gap
Diagnosing the actual cause of being stuck is the real mentoring skill, more than any single fixed technique

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows deliberate reasoning about the telling-vs-guiding tradeoff, not a default habit
Correctly diagnoses different causes of being stuck and adapts approach accordingly
Addresses the engineer's morale/confidence, not just the technical gap
Gives a specific, concrete example rather than abstract philosophy

questions.title: Disagreeing With a Peer's Technical Approach and Reaching Disagree-and-Commit
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you strongly disagreed with a peer's technical approach on something that mattered, made your case, and still lost the argument -- and had to commit to their approach anyway. How did you actually handle that, both in the moment and afterward?
questions.modelAnswer:
The thing this question is really testing is whether 'disagree and commit' is a genuine practice for the candidate or just a phrase they know to say -- and the tell is almost always in the specifics of what happened after losing the argument, not in how reasonably they describe disagreeing in the first place. A candidate who describes making their case clearly, losing, and then quietly undermining the chosen approach (bringing it up again in a different meeting, being visibly unenthusiastic in a way that signals to the team they think it's the wrong call, saying 'I told you so' energy once problems surface) is describing disagree-and-complain, not disagree-and-commit, and that pattern is a real red flag for Staff-level collaboration regardless of how the disagreement itself was handled.

A strong answer describes genuinely committing: actually putting full effort into making the chosen approach succeed, not a half-hearted technically-compliant minimum, and being honest about whether that was hard to do authentically or came easily once the decision was made. Equally important is what happened if the approach they disagreed with later ran into the exact problems they'd predicted -- a mature answer treats that as useful information to bring back calmly and constructively ('this is the issue I was concerned about, here's what we're seeing, what do we want to do about it') rather than as vindication to score points with, and the best answers acknowledge the genuine possibility that they were wrong to disagree in the first place, since losing an argument doesn't always mean the better argument lost, and a candidate who's certain, in hindsight, that they were right the whole time is worth a bit of skepticism.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd pick an example where I actually lost a real argument on something that mattered, not a minor stylistic preference, because the interesting part of this question is what happened after, not how reasonably I made my case beforehand. I'd want to be honest about whether committing was actually easy or hard for me in that specific case -- I think it's more credible to admit it was hard and describe what I did about that, than to claim I flipped a switch and felt totally aligned the moment the decision was made.

The part I'd focus on most is what actually committing looked like in practice -- did I put real effort into making the chosen approach succeed, or did I do the technically-compliant minimum while quietly signaling to the team that I thought it was the wrong call. I think the second one is disagree-and-complain, not disagree-and-commit, and I'd want to be honest if there's ever been a time I slipped into that, because I think everyone has at some point.

And if the approach I'd disagreed with later did run into a problem I'd predicted, I'd want to describe handling that calmly and constructively -- bringing it back as useful information, not as a moment to be right -- and I'd also want to be honest that losing an argument doesn't always mean I was actually correct in the first place; I'd try to acknowledge genuinely whether, in hindsight, the decision that won out was actually the better one.
commonMistakes: Describing disagree-and-commit as only the disagreement phase, with no account of what happened afterward
Describing quietly undermining the chosen approach after losing the argument (disagree-and-complain, not commit)
Claiming commitment came easily and authentically with no honest acknowledgment of difficulty
Treating a later vindication of the original concern as a chance to score points rather than useful information
Expressing certainty in hindsight that they were right all along, with no genuine consideration they may have been wrong
keyPoints: The real test of disagree-and-commit is behavior after losing the argument, not how the disagreement itself was handled
Quietly undermining a chosen approach after losing is disagree-and-complain, a meaningful failure mode to recognize
Genuine commitment means real effort toward the chosen approach's success, not a technically-compliant minimum
If a predicted problem later surfaces, raising it calmly and constructively is the mature response, not vindication-seeking
A credible answer acknowledges the real possibility that losing the argument meant being wrong, not just outvoted

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a real, substantive disagreement, not a minor preference
Gives honest, specific account of what genuine commitment looked like afterward
Avoids disagree-and-complain patterns; handles later vindication constructively if mentioned
Shows genuine humility about possibly having been wrong

questions.title: Communicating a Technical Risk to a Stakeholder Who Wants to Ship Anyway
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you identified a real technical risk in an AI feature -- something with genuine potential for harm or failure, not a nice-to-have improvement -- and had to communicate it to a non-technical stakeholder who was motivated to ship despite the risk. How did you handle that conversation, and what was the actual outcome?
questions.modelAnswer:
The core skill being tested is translating a technical risk into terms a non-technical stakeholder can actually weigh, without either dumbing it down to the point of being misleading or burying it in jargon that lets the stakeholder nod along without really understanding what they're agreeing to ship -- and a strong answer describes the specific translation they made, not just 'I explained the risk clearly,' which is a claim, not evidence. A good concrete translation connects the technical risk to something the stakeholder already cares about in their own terms: not 'the hallucination rate on this eval set is elevated' but 'roughly one in twenty customer-facing answers on this feature could state something false with full confidence, and here's a specific example of what that looked like in testing' -- grounding the abstract risk in a believable concrete scenario is usually what actually changes a stakeholder's calculus, more than the raw metric.

The honest and more interesting part of this question is the outcome, because it doesn't always go the way the engineer wanted, and a credible answer accounts for that possibility rather than always ending in 'and then they agreed with me and we delayed the launch.' A mature answer describes what happened if the stakeholder decided to ship anyway despite understanding the risk -- which is sometimes the right business call even with real risk acknowledged, if it's genuinely their call to make and they made it with full information -- and what the engineer did in that case: documenting the risk and the decision explicitly, putting monitoring in place specifically for that risk so it would be caught quickly if it materialized, and not treating 'I was overruled' as the end of their responsibility, since a Staff-level engineer's job isn't just to flag the risk once, it's to make sure the decision, whatever it is, is made with eyes open and with a plan for what happens if it goes wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd want to describe the specific way I translated the risk into terms the stakeholder could actually weigh, not just claim I 'explained it clearly,' because that's the part that actually shows whether I handled this well. The translation I'd aim for connects to something they already care about, in concrete terms -- not a raw eval metric, but something like 'about one in twenty customer-facing answers here could state something false with full confidence, and here's a specific real example from testing of what that looked like,' because a believable concrete scenario is usually what actually shifts someone's thinking, more than a number on a dashboard.

I'd also want to be honest about the outcome, because I don't think every one of these stories should end with 'and then they agreed with me.' If I'm being honest, sometimes the stakeholder heard the risk clearly, understood it, and decided to ship anyway, and that's genuinely their call to make if it's within their authority and they made it with real information, not because I failed to communicate. What I'd focus on in that case is what I did afterward -- documenting the risk and the decision explicitly so there's a real record, and putting specific monitoring in place for exactly that risk so if it did materialize, we'd catch it fast rather than finding out from a customer complaint. I don't think my job ends at flagging the risk once; I think it includes making sure whatever decision gets made is made with eyes open and has a plan if things go wrong.
commonMistakes: Claiming the risk was 'explained clearly' without describing the specific concrete translation used
Translating the risk using only technical jargon or raw metrics that don't actually connect to the stakeholder's own concerns
Describing an outcome that always ends in the stakeholder agreeing, with no honest account of being overruled
Treating being overruled as the end of responsibility, with no follow-up documentation or monitoring plan
Not acknowledging that shipping despite a known risk can be a legitimate business decision if made with full information
keyPoints: A strong answer describes a specific concrete translation of the risk, not just a claim of clear communication
Grounding an abstract risk in a believable concrete scenario is usually more persuasive than a raw metric alone
A credible answer accounts for the real possibility of being overruled, not just agreement
Shipping with a known, understood risk can be a legitimate stakeholder decision, not necessarily a communication failure
Responsibility continues after being overruled: documenting the decision and monitoring for the specific risk materializing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a specific, concrete risk translation rather than a vague claim
Gives an honest, credible account of the actual outcome, including possible override
Shows follow-through (documentation, monitoring) regardless of outcome
Acknowledges shipping with known risk can be a legitimate stakeholder decision

questions.title: Owning an Incident Postmortem and Driving the Follow-Up Actions
questions.prompt: Walk me through an incident you personally owned the postmortem for -- not just attended, but were responsible for writing up and driving to resolution. What went into the postmortem itself, and more importantly, how did you make sure the follow-up actions actually happened instead of becoming a list nobody revisits?
questions.modelAnswer:
The distinguishing signal in this question is almost entirely in the second half -- how follow-through actually worked -- because writing a reasonable postmortem document itself is a fairly standard, learnable skill, while making sure action items actually get done months later, after the incident's urgency has faded and everyone's attention has moved to the next thing, is the part that separates a postmortem that changes anything from one that's a well-written document nobody acts on. A candidate should describe the postmortem's content honestly, including a blameless but specific account of root cause (not vague language like 'a confluence of factors' that avoids naming what actually went wrong), and should be able to name the actual timeline and contributing factors concretely enough that someone reading it a year later understands what happened without having been there.

The stronger half of the answer is the mechanism for follow-through: did action items get assigned to specific named owners with real due dates, not a list of good intentions with no accountability attached; was there a recurring check-in (a standing review of open postmortem action items, not a one-time mention in a retro that never gets revisited) that surfaced items that were stalling; and critically, did the candidate personally push on items that were behind schedule rather than treating 'I wrote the postmortem and assigned the actions' as the end of their job. The best answers also include an honest account of at least one action item that didn't get done on time or at all, and what that revealed -- either about prioritization, about the item being less important than it seemed in the heat of the incident, or about a real accountability gap worth fixing -- because a postmortem process where every single action item always gets done on schedule is either a very small sample size or not being described candidly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd want to spend most of my answer on the follow-through, honestly, because writing the postmortem document itself isn't the hard part -- walking through root cause, timeline, contributing factors, blamelessly but specifically, is a skill most people can learn fairly quickly. What actually separates a postmortem that changes something from one that just sits in a wiki is whether the action items get done, and that's the part I'd focus on describing concretely.

I'd talk about making sure every action item had a specific named owner and a real due date, not just a list of good intentions with nobody actually accountable for them. And I'd describe a recurring check-in -- not a one-time mention in a retro that nobody revisits, but an actual standing review of open action items -- because that's what surfaces the ones quietly stalling before they're forgotten entirely. I'd also be honest that part of my job in that process was personally pushing on items that were falling behind, not assuming that assigning an owner once was enough.

And I'd want to be candid that not everything got done on time -- I'd describe a specific action item that slipped or never happened, and what that actually told us, whether it was a real prioritization call, the item turning out to be less critical than it felt in the moment of the incident, or an actual gap in how we were holding people accountable. I think a postmortem story where literally everything always got done on schedule either hasn't happened to me yet or isn't being told completely honestly.
commonMistakes: Spending most of the answer on the postmortem document's content rather than the follow-through mechanism
Using vague, non-specific root-cause language that avoids naming what actually went wrong
Describing action items with no named owner or due date, just a list of good intentions
Having no recurring check-in mechanism, relying on a one-time retro mention that's never revisited
Claiming every action item was completed on schedule with no honest account of anything slipping
keyPoints: The real differentiator is the follow-through mechanism, not the postmortem document's writing quality
Root cause should be described specifically and blamelessly, not with vague hand-waving language
Action items need named owners and real due dates to create actual accountability
A recurring standing review (not a one-time retro mention) is needed to surface stalling action items
An honest account should include at least one action item that slipped, and what that revealed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a specific, concrete postmortem with honest, non-vague root cause
Describes a real follow-through mechanism (owners, due dates, recurring review)
Shows personal accountability for pushing on stalled items
Gives an honest account of at least one item that slipped and what it revealed

deepDive.heading: Why postmortem quality is measured months later, not at write-time
deepDive.content: A postmortem's real test isn't how it reads the week it's published, when the incident is fresh and everyone's attention is on it. It's whether, six months later, the action items it generated actually happened and the same failure mode doesn't recur. Most postmortem processes fail quietly at exactly this point: the document is good, the meeting where it's reviewed is thoughtful, and then organizational attention moves on and half the action items never close. Evaluating this answer means specifically listening for whether the candidate's story holds up past the write-time phase.

deepDive.heading: The blameless-but-specific balance
deepDive.content: A genuinely useful postmortem has to be blameless (focused on systems and process gaps, not individual failing) while still being specific enough to be actionable (naming the exact config value, the exact missing check, the exact assumption that was wrong). Candidates sometimes over-correct toward blamelessness and end up with root-cause language so soft it doesn't actually point at anything fixable -- 'a confluence of factors contributed to the incident' is blameless but useless. The better version names the specific gap: 'the deploy pipeline did not include a step that would have caught this' is blameless and specific at the same time.

deepDive.heading: What good follow-through accountability actually looks like
deepDive.content: The mechanism that reliably works across organizations is boring and specific: every action item gets a named owner (a person, not a team) and a real due date at write-time, not 'eventually.' Open items get reviewed on a standing cadence separate from the original incident review -- weekly or biweekly, visible to the owner's manager, not buried in a doc nobody reopens. And someone (often the postmortem owner) has explicit responsibility for escalating items that are behind schedule, rather than assuming visibility alone creates urgency.

deepDive.heading: Why an honest 'something slipped' answer is actually the stronger signal
deepDive.content: A candidate who claims a flawless 100% action-item completion rate across every postmortem they've run is either describing a very small sample or not being fully candid, and either way it's a weaker answer than someone who can describe a specific item that didn't get done, what that revealed about priorities or accountability, and what they changed in the process as a result. The willingness to name a real failure in their own follow-through process is itself evidence of the kind of ownership this question is trying to assess.

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Roadmap Ask That Skips Necessary Safety Work
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time product or leadership wanted to ship an AI feature on a timeline that skipped safety/guardrail work you believed was necessary. How did you push back, and how did you balance being a good partner to the business with not compromising on something you thought mattered?
questions.modelAnswer:
The core tension this question probes is whether the candidate can push back effectively without either being a pushover (going along with a timeline they genuinely believe is unsafe, just to avoid friction) or being obstructionist (treating every timeline pressure as something to resist regardless of actual risk, which erodes the trust needed to be heard the next time something really does matter) -- and the strongest answers show they can tell the difference and calibrate accordingly. A good answer describes making the actual risk concrete and specific rather than appealing to a vague standard ('we should always do thorough safety review'), because a specific, scoped articulation of what could go wrong and how likely or severe it is gives leadership something real to weigh against the timeline pressure, rather than asking them to just trust a general principle.

The more interesting and differentiating part of the answer is whether the candidate found or proposed a middle path rather than framing it as a binary 'ship on time with no safety work' versus 'delay the whole launch' -- a strong answer often describes negotiating a scoped-down but real safety measure that could actually be done in the available time (a narrower guardrail covering the highest-risk failure mode specifically, rather than the full comprehensive version, shipped alongside a committed follow-up timeline for the rest) rather than treating the safety work as all-or-nothing. And a genuinely strong answer is honest about what happened if the push-back didn't fully succeed -- if leadership decided to ship with less safety work than the candidate wanted, what did they do next: document the accepted risk explicitly, build monitoring specifically to catch that risk's specific failure mode fast, and continue advocating for the remaining work in a follow-up rather than treating a partial loss as total defeat or using it as grounds to disengage.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd want to show that I can tell the difference between a timeline pressure I should push back on hard and one I should accept, because I don't think treating every deadline as something to resist is actually good partnership with the business -- that erodes trust and makes it harder to be heard the next time something really does matter. So I'd describe making the actual risk concrete and specific, not appealing to a general 'we should always be thorough about safety' principle, because a vague standard doesn't give leadership anything real to weigh -- I'd want to describe the specific failure mode, how likely it felt, and what the actual consequence would be if it happened.

The part I'd focus on most is finding a middle path rather than treating this as all-or-nothing. Instead of 'ship with zero safety work' versus 'delay the whole launch,' I'd describe negotiating something narrower but real -- a guardrail covering specifically the highest-risk failure mode, shippable in the available time, with a committed follow-up timeline for the more comprehensive version, rather than insisting on the full scope upfront or giving up on safety work entirely.

And I'd be honest if the pushback didn't fully succeed -- if leadership ultimately decided to ship with less than I wanted, I'd describe what I did next: documenting that accepted risk explicitly so it's a real decision on record, building monitoring specifically aimed at catching that exact failure mode fast if it did materialize, and continuing to advocate for the remaining work afterward rather than treating a partial loss as the end of the conversation.
commonMistakes: Treating every timeline pressure as something to resist regardless of actual risk severity
Appealing to a vague general safety principle instead of articulating the specific, scoped risk at stake
Framing the situation as strictly binary (full safety work vs. none) instead of proposing a scoped middle path
Giving up entirely or disengaging after a partial loss instead of documenting the risk and continuing to advocate
Not describing concrete follow-up monitoring for the specific risk that was accepted
keyPoints: Effective pushback distinguishes real, severe risk from reflexive resistance to any timeline pressure
Articulating a specific, scoped risk is more persuasive to leadership than appealing to a general safety principle
A scoped middle-path proposal (partial safety work now, committed follow-up) is often more effective than an all-or-nothing stance
A credible answer accounts for the possibility of a partial loss, not just full success
Continued advocacy and targeted monitoring after a partial loss show ownership beyond the initial pushback

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows calibrated judgment distinguishing real risk from reflexive resistance
Describes a specific, concrete risk rather than a vague principle
Proposes or negotiates a scoped middle path rather than an all-or-nothing framing
Gives an honest account of handling a partial loss, including follow-up monitoring/advocacy

questions.title: Negotiating Scope When a Request Isn't Technically Feasible on the Timeline
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time product asked for an AI feature that, as specified, genuinely wasn't achievable on the timeline they wanted -- not a matter of working harder, an actual technical constraint. How did you handle that conversation, and what did you propose instead of just saying no?
questions.modelAnswer:
A weak version of this answer is just 'I explained it wasn't possible and they accepted that,' because that's a low-value contribution from a Staff-level engineer -- saying no to an infeasible request is the easy part; the actual value is in proposing a workable alternative that gets product most of what they actually need within the real constraint, which requires understanding what they're actually trying to achieve (the underlying business goal) well enough to propose a different path to it, not just defending why the originally specified path is broken. A strong answer describes digging into the actual underlying need behind the request -- often the specific feature as initially specified was one implementation of a broader goal, and there's a narrower or differently-shaped version of that goal that is achievable on the timeline, even if it's not identical to what was literally asked for.

The credibility of the answer depends heavily on specificity: a vague 'we found a compromise that worked for everyone' is a much weaker signal than naming the actual technical constraint precisely (why, specifically, was the original ask infeasible -- a model capability limitation, a data availability gap, a latency requirement that's physically incompatible with the approach needed for quality) and the actual alternative proposed, concretely, with the reasoning for why it addresses the real underlying goal. The best answers also show the candidate brought options rather than a single alternative, giving product a real choice (a narrower version shippable on time, versus the full version on a longer timeline) rather than presenting 'here's the one thing I'll let you have' -- because framing it as a genuine choice respects that the business tradeoff (speed vs. completeness) is ultimately product's call to make once they understand the real constraint, not the engineer's call to make for them.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd want to go past 'I explained it wasn't feasible and they accepted it,' because that part is actually the easy half of this -- the real value I'd want to show is in the alternative I proposed, not just correctly identifying the constraint. So I'd describe digging into what product was actually trying to accomplish underneath the specific feature they asked for, because usually the literal request is one way to get a broader goal, and there's often a narrower or differently-shaped version of that same goal that's genuinely achievable in the time they have, even if it's not identical to what they originally described.

I'd be specific about the actual technical constraint, not vague -- naming exactly why the original ask wasn't feasible, whether that's a model capability limit, a data gap, or a latency requirement that's physically at odds with the quality bar needed -- because a vague 'we found something that worked' doesn't actually demonstrate I understood the constraint well enough to navigate around it credibly.

And I'd want to describe bringing more than one option, not just the single alternative I personally preferred -- something like a narrower version shippable on their original timeline, versus the full version on a realistic longer timeline -- because I think that tradeoff between speed and completeness is genuinely product's call to make once they understand the real constraint clearly, not a decision I should be making for them by only presenting the one option I'd already decided on.
commonMistakes: Framing the answer as just 'I said it wasn't feasible and they accepted it' with no concrete alternative proposed
Not digging into the underlying business goal behind the specific feature request before proposing an alternative
Describing the resolution vaguely ('we found a compromise') without naming the specific technical constraint
Presenting only a single predetermined alternative instead of giving product a real choice between options
Making the speed-vs-completeness tradeoff decision unilaterally instead of letting product choose with full information
keyPoints: Explaining infeasibility alone is the low-value half of this situation; proposing a workable alternative is the real contribution
Understanding the underlying business goal behind a specific request enables a credible alternative proposal
Specificity about the actual technical constraint (not a vague compromise) demonstrates real understanding
Presenting multiple options respects that the speed-vs-completeness tradeoff is ultimately the business's decision
A credible answer shows navigating around a real constraint, not just identifying that one exists

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Goes beyond explaining infeasibility to a concrete, workable alternative
Shows understanding of the underlying business goal, not just the literal request
Names the specific technical constraint precisely rather than vaguely
Presents multiple options, respecting the business's right to choose the tradeoff

questions.title: Setting Engineering Standards Across a Team
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you introduced or changed an engineering standard -- a code review bar, a required practice for shipping AI features, a documentation requirement -- across a team, not just for your own work. How did you get buy-in, and how did you handle the person or people who resisted it?
questions.modelAnswer:
A weak answer describes a standard being declared or mandated with no account of how buy-in was actually built, which is a real problem because a standard that's imposed without buy-in tends to get followed in letter but not spirit -- people check the box without understanding or believing in why it matters, which means the standard quietly erodes the first time it's inconvenient. A strong answer describes starting from the actual problem the standard was meant to solve, made concrete (a specific incident, a specific recurring quality issue) rather than introducing the standard as an abstract best practice, because people buy into solving a problem they recognize far more readily than they buy into a rule for its own sake.

The more revealing part of the answer is how resistance was actually handled, because resistance to a new standard is common and not inherently a bad sign -- sometimes it reflects a legitimate cost or edge case the standard didn't account for, and a candidate who describes steamrolling all resistance as stubbornness to overcome, rather than engaging with whether some of it was valid, is missing an important distinction. A strong answer describes actually listening to the substance of resistance, adjusting the standard where the pushback revealed a real gap (an exception case, a lighter-weight version for low-risk situations), and only holding firm where the resistance was really about preferring the old, easier way rather than a substantive objection -- and ideally describes a specific person whose resistance was handled well, with a concrete account of what changed their mind (or what accommodation was made for them) rather than a vague 'eventually everyone came around.'
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd want to start the story from the actual problem the standard was meant to fix, made concrete -- a specific incident or a specific recurring issue -- rather than describing myself introducing an abstract best practice, because I think people genuinely buy into solving a problem they recognize far more than they buy into a new rule just because it sounds like good practice. So I'd walk through what the real, visible pain point was that made this standard worth introducing in the first place.

On resistance, I'd want to be honest that not all of it was wrong, and I think that's actually the more interesting part of the story. I'd describe listening to the substance of the pushback and actually adjusting the standard where it revealed something real I hadn't accounted for -- maybe an exception case, or a lighter version for lower-risk situations -- rather than treating every objection as something to just overcome through persistence. And I'd want to describe one specific person whose resistance I handled directly, with a concrete account of what actually changed their mind or what accommodation I made, rather than a vague 'eventually everyone came around,' because that specific detail is what shows I actually engaged with the resistance rather than just waiting it out.
commonMistakes: Describing the standard as mandated/declared with no account of how buy-in was actually built
Introducing the standard as an abstract best practice rather than grounding it in a concrete, recognized problem
Treating all resistance as stubbornness to overcome rather than engaging with whether some objections were valid
Not adjusting the standard at all in response to legitimate pushback, applying it rigidly regardless of edge cases
Giving a vague 'eventually everyone came around' account with no specific person or concrete resolution detail
keyPoints: Grounding a new standard in a concrete, recognized problem builds more genuine buy-in than an abstract best-practice pitch
A standard imposed without buy-in tends to be followed in letter but not spirit, eroding over time
Resistance to a new standard is not inherently invalid and sometimes reveals a real gap worth addressing
Adjusting the standard for legitimate edge cases, while holding firm against mere preference for the old way, shows good judgment
A specific, concrete account of handling one resistant person is more credible than a vague general claim

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Grounds the standard in a concrete, recognized problem rather than an abstract pitch
Engages genuinely with resistance rather than treating it all as stubbornness
Describes adjusting the standard where pushback revealed a real gap
Gives a specific, concrete account of handling a resistant individual

questions.title: Deciding When to Pay Down Technical Debt vs. Ship
questions.prompt: Tell me about a real decision you made (or strongly influenced) about whether to pay down technical debt now versus ship a feature on schedule and deal with the debt later. What factors actually drove that decision, and were you right?
questions.modelAnswer:
A weak answer treats this as a binary philosophical stance ('I always prioritize paying down debt' or 'I always prioritize shipping'), because neither extreme is actually good judgment -- the real skill being tested is whether the candidate can articulate the specific factors that actually drove a real decision: how much is this specific debt actually compounding (is it making every future change in this area measurably slower, or is it localized and not actually blocking anything yet), how reversible is the decision to defer it (can it realistically be paid down later without much more cost, or does shipping on top of it lock in a much more expensive future refactor), and what's the actual cost of the delay to ship now versus the business value of hitting the current deadline, stated in real terms rather than a vague 'the business wants it.'

The most valuable part of the answer is the honest retrospective -- 'were you right' is specifically asked because a candidate willing to say 'no, I was wrong, here's what actually happened and what I'd do differently' demonstrates more judgment than one who claims perfect hindsight validation every time, which is an implausible claim at Staff level making real tradeoffs regularly. A strong answer describes the actual outcome concretely: if they chose to ship and defer debt, did the deferred debt actually get paid down later as planned, or did it compound further because 'later' never came (a very common and worth-naming failure mode); if they chose to pay down debt first, was the delay to shipping actually worth it in retrospect, or did it turn out to be less critical than it felt at the time. Either honest outcome, examined candidly, is a stronger answer than a story that conveniently confirms the original decision was perfect.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd avoid making this a philosophical stance, because I don't think 'always pay down debt first' or 'always ship on schedule' is actually good judgment -- I'd want to walk through the specific factors that drove a real decision I made. I'd talk about how much that particular debt was actually compounding -- was it genuinely slowing down every change in that area, or was it localized and not actually blocking anything yet -- and how reversible deferring it really was, because debt that gets measurably more expensive to pay down the longer it sits is a very different call than debt that's fine to leave for a while. And I'd want to state the actual cost of delay versus the real business value of the deadline in concrete terms, not just 'the business wanted it.'

The part I'd be most honest about is whether I was actually right, because I think claiming perfect hindsight validation every time isn't believable for anyone making these calls regularly. I'd describe the real outcome -- if I chose to ship and defer, did that debt actually get paid down later like we planned, or did 'later' never really come and it compounded further, which I think is a really common failure mode worth naming honestly. Or if I chose to pay the debt down first, I'd be honest about whether that delay was actually worth it in retrospect, or whether the thing felt more urgent in the moment than it turned out to matter.
commonMistakes: Treating the decision as a fixed philosophical stance rather than factors weighed for this specific case
Not articulating how much the specific debt was actually compounding or how reversible deferring it was
Stating business value/cost only vaguely ('the business wanted it') instead of in concrete terms
Claiming the original decision was perfectly validated in hindsight with no honest account of being wrong
Not naming the common failure mode where deferred debt never actually gets paid down later as planned
keyPoints: Good debt-vs-ship judgment weighs specific factors (compounding rate, reversibility, concrete cost/value) rather than a fixed stance
Debt that compounds faster the longer it's deferred is a materially different case than debt that's safe to leave
An honest retrospective, including admitting being wrong, is a stronger signal than claimed perfect hindsight validation
A common real failure mode is deferred debt never actually getting paid down because 'later' never comes
The business cost/value comparison should be stated in concrete terms, not a vague appeal to business priority

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Articulates specific decision factors rather than a fixed philosophical stance
States cost/value tradeoffs concretely rather than vaguely
Gives an honest retrospective, including the possibility of having been wrong
Names the realistic failure mode of deferred debt never actually being paid down

questions.title: Roadmapping a Business Goal Into a Technical Plan
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you took a business-level goal that wasn't yet a technical plan -- something like 'reduce support ticket volume by 20% this quarter' or 'expand into a new customer segment' -- and turned it into an actual engineering roadmap for an AI feature or platform capability. Walk through how you made that translation.
questions.modelAnswer:
A weak answer jumps straight to a technical solution without describing the translation step itself, which is actually the valuable skill being probed here -- a business goal like 'reduce support ticket volume by 20%' doesn't specify which tickets, why they're happening, or whether an AI feature is even the right lever, so a strong answer describes investigating the actual goal first: what's driving the current ticket volume (is it a specific category of question, a specific product area, a specific customer segment), and whether the proposed AI intervention is actually likely to move that specific driver, rather than reaching for 'build an AI assistant' as a generic answer to any support-cost goal without first confirming the problem shape actually fits that solution.

The translation into an actual roadmap should show explicit reasoning connecting engineering work to the business metric, not just a list of features that sound related: a credible roadmap states which specific engineering milestones are expected to move the metric, by roughly how much and by when, with the reasoning for that connection made explicit (if 40% of ticket volume is billing questions and an assistant can deflect a meaningfully high fraction of those based on a pilot or comparable benchmark, that's a stated, falsifiable link, versus a roadmap that lists shipping a feature and hopes the metric moves). The strongest answers also describe building in a checkpoint to verify the assumption against real data partway through rather than only at the end -- since the initial translation from business goal to technical plan always rests on assumptions (which ticket categories are deflectable, how much the AI feature will actually reduce them) that should be checked against real data as early as possible, adjusting the roadmap if the data doesn't support the original assumption rather than running the full plan to completion on a premise that turned out to be wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd want to describe the translation step itself clearly, because I think that's actually the hard and valuable part here, not jumping straight to a technical solution. A goal like 'reduce support ticket volume by 20%' doesn't on its own tell you which tickets, why they're happening, or even whether an AI feature is the right lever at all -- so I'd walk through investigating the actual driver first: what category of question is actually generating the volume, which product area or customer segment it's concentrated in, and whether an AI intervention is actually likely to move that specific driver rather than defaulting to 'build an assistant' as a generic answer to any cost-reduction goal.

For the actual roadmap, I'd want to show explicit reasoning connecting the engineering milestones to the business metric, not just a list of features that sound relevant. Something like: if a meaningful share of ticket volume is a specific category of question, and a pilot or comparable benchmark suggests an assistant can deflect a real fraction of those, that's a stated, checkable link between the work and the metric -- versus just shipping something and hoping the number moves.

And I'd specifically describe building in a checkpoint partway through to verify that assumption against real data, because the whole translation from business goal to technical plan rests on an assumption that could turn out to be wrong, and I'd rather catch that early and adjust the roadmap than run the full plan to completion on a premise that didn't actually hold up once we had real numbers.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to a technical solution without describing the investigation into what actually drives the business metric
Defaulting to a generic AI feature as the answer without confirming the problem shape actually fits that solution
Presenting a roadmap as a list of features without explicit, stated reasoning connecting the work to the business metric
Making the connection between engineering work and the metric unfalsifiable (no stated expected impact or timeline)
Running the full roadmap to completion with no checkpoint to verify the underlying assumption against real data
keyPoints: Translating a business goal into a technical plan requires investigating what's actually driving the metric first
An AI feature should be validated as the right lever for the specific driver, not assumed by default
A credible roadmap states an explicit, falsifiable connection between engineering milestones and the business metric
Building in an early checkpoint to verify the underlying assumption against real data prevents running a flawed plan to completion
The roadmap should be adjusted if real data doesn't support the original assumption, not followed rigidly regardless

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes investigating the actual business-metric driver before proposing a technical solution
Shows explicit, falsifiable reasoning connecting engineering work to the business metric
Includes an early checkpoint to verify assumptions against real data
Avoids defaulting to a generic AI solution without validating fit

questions.title: Giving Difficult Feedback on a Peer's Design in an Architecture Review
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to give genuinely difficult, critical feedback on a peer's design in a formal architecture review -- not a minor suggestion, but feedback that meant significant rework or even questioned whether the approach should proceed at all. How did you deliver that feedback, and how did the peer actually receive it?
questions.modelAnswer:
A weak answer describes only the content of the technical objection without any account of how it was delivered, because delivery is the actual skill being tested here -- the same substantive feedback can land as constructive and respected or as dismissive and damaging depending entirely on how it's framed, and a Staff-level engineer needs to be good at the delivery, not just correct on the substance. A strong answer describes specific choices made in how the feedback was framed: addressing the design and its tradeoffs rather than the person, being specific about the actual technical concern rather than a vague 'this doesn't feel right,' and -- importantly -- acknowledging genuine strengths of the design where they existed rather than presenting the feedback as wholesale rejection when the actual concern was narrower, since overstating the severity of feedback erodes trust just as much as understating it.

The more revealing part of the answer is how the peer actually received it, and a credible answer doesn't always describe a perfectly smooth reception -- acknowledging that the peer was initially defensive, disappointed, or needed time to process significant critical feedback before engaging productively with it is more believable and more informative than a story where everyone immediately thanked the candidate for their insight. What separates a strong answer is what the candidate did in response to that initial reaction: giving the peer space and time rather than pushing for immediate agreement in the room, following up privately rather than only addressing it in the public review setting, and checking in afterward on the working relationship specifically, not just whether the technical concern got resolved -- because difficult feedback that's technically correct but damages a peer relationship long-term is a real cost that a Staff-level engineer should be actively managing, not an acceptable side effect of being right.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd want to spend real time on how I actually delivered the feedback, not just what the technical objection was, because I think the delivery is the part that's actually hard and actually the skill being tested here -- the exact same substantive point can land completely differently depending on how it's framed. I'd describe specifically addressing the design and its tradeoffs rather than anything about the person, being precise about the actual concern rather than something vague like 'this doesn't feel right,' and making sure I named real strengths in the design where they existed, because I don't think overstating how bad the feedback is does anyone any favors -- that erodes trust just as much as sugarcoating a real problem would.

I'd also want to be honest about how my peer actually reacted, because I don't think every story like this ends with someone immediately thanking you for the insight -- I'd describe if there was some initial defensiveness or disappointment, because significant critical feedback on something someone's put real work into is genuinely hard to hear in the moment, and pretending otherwise isn't credible.

What I'd focus on is what I did after that initial reaction -- giving them space rather than pushing for immediate agreement right there in the review, following up privately afterward rather than only ever addressing it in the public setting, and specifically checking in later on how we were doing as colleagues, not just whether the technical issue itself got resolved. I think feedback that's technically right but quietly damages a working relationship is a real cost, and managing that is part of the job, not something I get to shrug off because I was correct.
commonMistakes: Describing only the technical content of the feedback with no account of how it was actually delivered
Framing the feedback around the person rather than the design and its specific tradeoffs
Overstating the severity of the feedback, presenting a narrower concern as wholesale rejection
Claiming the peer immediately and smoothly accepted difficult feedback with no honest account of initial reaction
Treating the technical resolution as the end of the matter with no follow-up on the working relationship
keyPoints: Delivery and framing matter as much as the substance of difficult feedback, and are the real skill being assessed
Addressing the design and specific tradeoffs, not the person, is a key framing choice
Acknowledging genuine strengths prevents overstating the severity of narrower concerns
A credible account acknowledges the peer's initial defensiveness or disappointment rather than a uniformly smooth reception
Following up privately and checking in on the working relationship afterward shows ownership beyond being technically correct

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Focuses substantively on delivery/framing, not just the technical content
Describes specific, concrete framing choices (design not person, specific not vague, strengths acknowledged)
Gives an honest, credible account of the peer's actual reaction
Shows follow-up care for the working relationship, not just technical resolution
